C-130 has a wider fuselage than the C-47.

C-47: C-47 has a low-wing configuration with wings mounted near the bottom of the fuselage.

C-47 has a blunt, rounded nose profile without a stepped cockpit or glazed bombardier position.

C-47 has a narrow cylindrical fuselage cross-section with smooth tapering from nose to tail.

C-47 has a shorter fuselage than the DC-6, which appears noticeably longer and more streamlined.
C-47 has a smaller overall size and lower height than the An-12, especially at the tail and engine nacelles.
C-47 lacks the high-mounted T-tail found on the C-130 and instead has a conventional low-set tailplane.
C-47 has no cargo ramp door at the rear—its main cargo door is on the left side amidships.
C-47 has a rounded, unbroken fuselage contour without the pronounced dorsal hump of the DC-6.
C-47 has smaller-diameter engine nacelles compared to the larger, more elongated nacelles of the DC-6.
C-47 has no turboprop engines—its powerplants are visibly radial piston engines with exposed cylinders.
C-47 has a narrower wingspan relative to fuselage length than the C-130, giving it a more compact appearance.
C-47 has no winglets or wingtip devices, distinguishing it from modern derivatives like some DC-3 conversions.
C-47 has a simple, uncluttered wing trailing edge with no flaps extending beyond the wingtips, unlike later transports.
C-47 has a cockpit canopy with multiple small, flat panes arranged in a curved but non-bulging layout.
C-47 has no auxiliary air intakes or cooling gills on the fuselage, unlike the An-12’s prominent chin intake.
C-47 has a single, continuous dorsal fairing running from cockpit to tail, without the segmented spine of the DC-6.
CRJ-200: CRJ-200 has a shorter fuselage than the CRJ-700 and CRJ-900.
CRJ-200 features twin rear-mounted turbofan engines positioned on either side of the aft fuselage.
CRJ-200 has a T-tail configuration with the horizontal stabilizer mounted high on the vertical fin.
CRJ-200 has low-mounted swept wings with small wing-root fairings.
CRJ-200 has a long, narrow cylindrical fuselage with a pointed nose.
CRJ-200 has main landing gear mounted under the fuselage near the wing roots rather than in large wing pods.
CRJ-200 has smaller-diameter engines compared to the CRJ-700 and CRJ-900.
CRJ-200 has a single-aisle regional-jet proportion with relatively compact overall dimensions.
CRJ-200 lacks the stretched fuselage and enlarged cabin windows found on the CRJ-700.
CRJ-200 has a more tapered and slender nose profile than the ERJ 145.
CRJ-200 has no winglets, distinguishing it visually from later CRJ variants that sometimes feature them.
CRJ-200 has two passenger doors on the left side forward of the wing and one service door aft of the wing.
CRJ-200 has a narrower fuselage diameter than the ERJ 145.
CRJ-200 has a higher tail fin aspect ratio compared to the ERJ 135.
CRJ-200 has engine nacelles that sit closer to the fuselage than those on the CRJ-900.
CRJ-200 has a shorter distance between the nose and the leading edge of the wing than the CRJ-700.
CRJ-200 has a less pronounced wing sweep angle than the ERJ 145.
CRJ-200 has a smoother, uninterrupted fuselage contour without the mid-fuselage plug sections seen on the CRJ-700.
CRJ-200 has a cockpit glazing layout with a distinct five-panel windshield configuration unlike the ERJ series.
CRJ-200 has a smaller vertical tail surface area than the CRJ-900.
CRJ-700: CRJ-700 has a low-mounted swept wing with moderate sweep angle, distinct from the ERJ 145's less-swept wing.
CRJ-700 features two turbofan engines mounted on the rear fuselage, unlike the E-170's underwing engine placement.
CRJ-700 displays a T-tail empennage with a horizontal stabilizer mounted at the top of the vertical fin, differing from the CRJ-200's similar but shorter tail assembly.
CRJ-700 possesses a long, narrow cylindrical fuselage proportionally longer than the CRJ-200 but shorter than the CRJ-900.
CRJ-700 has a pointed nose and streamlined cockpit glazing, more elongated than the blunt-nosed ERJ 145.
CRJ-700 uses main landing gear housed in fairings along the fuselage sides, not extending from the wings like the E-170.
CRJ-700 exhibits a small vertical tail relative to overall fuselage length, visually more compact than the CRJ-900's taller tail.
CRJ-700 shows a single forward passenger door and a single overwing emergency exit on each side, differing from the CRJ-900's two overwing exits.
CRJ-700 has a fuselage cross-section that appears narrower in diameter than the E-170's wider cabin profile.
CRJ-700 features winglets that are shorter and less pronounced than those on the CRJ-900.
CRJ-700 displays a smooth, uninterrupted fuselage contour without the pronounced rear fuselage taper seen on the ERJ 145.
CRJ-700 has a cockpit windshield with five distinct panes arranged in a curved, forward-sloping layout, unlike the ERJ 145's flatter, four-pane arrangement.
CRJ-700 shows engine nacelles mounted directly to the rear fuselage with minimal gap between nacelle and skin, contrasting with the E-170's larger nacelle-to-fuselage clearance.
CRJ-700 has a rear pressure bulkhead located farther aft than on the CRJ-200, contributing to its visibly extended rear fuselage.
CRJ-700 features a dorsal fin extension ahead of the vertical stabilizer, more prominent than on the CRJ-200 but less so than on the CRJ-900.
CRJ-700 displays a wing root fairing that blends smoothly into the fuselage underside, lacking the pronounced bulge seen on the ERJ 145.
CRJ-700 has a forward fuselage that tapers gradually toward the nose, unlike the sharper taper of the CRJ-200.
CRJ-700 shows a ventral fin beneath the rear fuselage, smaller and less angled than the one on the CRJ-900.
CRJ-700 features a horizontal stabilizer with slight anhedral, whereas the ERJ 145's stabilizer is nearly level.
CRJ-700 has a main landing gear track width narrower than the E-170's, resulting in a tighter stance visible from front or rear views.
CRJ-900: CRJ-900 has a longer fuselage than the CRJ-700 and CRJ-200.
CRJ-900 features two rear-mounted turbofan engines, unlike the wing-mounted engines of the Boeing 737.
CRJ-900 has a T-tail configuration with a tall vertical fin and high-mounted horizontal stabilizer, distinguishing it from the conventional tail of the ERJ 145.
CRJ-900 has a low-wing layout, whereas the Embraer ERJ 145 also has a low wing but with a noticeably shorter fuselage and different tail proportions.
CRJ-900 has a pointed nose and streamlined cockpit profile, more elongated than the blunter nose of the CRJ-200.
CRJ-900 has main landing gear housed in streamlined fuselage fairings, not in large wing-mounted pods like the ATR 72.
CRJ-900 has a slender cylindrical fuselage with a narrow cross-section compared to the wider cabin of the E175.
CRJ-900 has wingtip extensions that are small and blended, unlike the larger winglets on later-generation regional jets such as the E190-E2.
CRJ-900 has a longer forward fuselage section ahead of the first passenger door than the CRJ-700.
CRJ-900 has two overwing emergency exits on each side, whereas the CRJ-200 has only one.
CRJ-900 has a taller vertical stabilizer relative to fuselage height than the CRJ-700.
CRJ-900 has a more pronounced rear fuselage taper than the CRJ-200.
CRJ-900 has engine nacelles mounted directly on the rear fuselage without pylons, unlike the pylon-mounted engines of the Airbus A220.
CRJ-900 has a single-piece, curved windshield with a steep rake, distinct from the flatter, multi-panel cockpit glass of the ERJ 145.
CRJ-900 has a longer distance between the nose gear and main gear than the CRJ-200.
CRJ-900 has a narrower chord horizontal stabilizer mounted high on the vertical fin, unlike the lower-mounted and broader stabilizer of the BAe 146.
CRJ-900 has a smooth, uninterrupted fuselage contour without external air conditioning packs protruding beneath the mid-fuselage, unlike some older regional jets.
CRJ-900 has a slightly greater wing sweep angle than the CRJ-200, visible in side profile.
CRJ-900 has a longer aft fuselage behind the wing than the CRJ-700.
CRJ-900 has a distinctive rear pressure bulkhead location just forward of the vertical fin base, creating a clean, tapered termination to the fuselage.
Cessna 172: Cessna 172 has a high-mounted straight wing with visible external struts connecting each wing to the lower fuselage.
Cessna 172 features fixed tricycle landing gear with non-retractable main wheels and a steerable nose wheel.
Cessna 172 has a single piston engine mounted in the nose driving a two- or three-blade propeller.
Cessna 172 has a slab-sided fuselage with a rounded, bulbous nose and simple general-aviation proportions.
Cessna 172 has a conventional tail configuration with a low-mounted horizontal stabilizer and a single vertical fin.
Cessna 172 has rectangular side cabin windows arranged in a single row along the mid-fuselage.
Cessna 172 has a shorter fuselage than the Cessna 208 Caravan.
Cessna 172 has a higher wing position than the PA-28 Cherokee, whose wing is mid-mounted.
Cessna 172 has no winglets or wingtip devices, unlike the SR-20.
Cessna 172 has a simpler, less tapered nose profile compared to the DR-400’s more pointed nose.
Cessna 172 has a single-piece, forward-hinged canopy over the front cockpit, not split or rear-hinged like some DR-400 variants.
Cessna 172 has a straight, unswept wing with no dihedral or anhedral visible in standard views.
Cessna 172 has a smaller overall footprint than the Cessna 208, especially in wingspan and length.
Cessna 172 has a fixed-pitch or constant-speed propeller, not a turboprop-driven multi-blade unit like the Cessna 208.
Cessna 172 has a single vertical tail surface without a dorsal fin extension, unlike later SR-20 models.
Cessna 172 has a flat, unfaired engine cowling with prominent cooling air intakes near the spinner.
Cessna 172 has a narrow, shallow fuselage cross-section compared to the deeper, wider cabin of the PA-28.
Cessna 172 has no wing-mounted pods or nacelles, distinguishing it from twin-engine aircraft like the PA-34.
Cessna 172 has a smooth, uninterrupted upper fuselage line without humps or raised avionics bays seen on some SR-20s.
Cessna 172 has a short, stubby tailcone ending in a simple rounded contour, not elongated or tapered like the DR-400’s.
Cessna 208: Cessna 208 has a high-mounted straight wing with prominent external strut bracing connecting to the lower fuselage.
Cessna 208 features a single turboprop engine mounted in the nose, unlike the jet engines of the Cessna 525 and Cessna 560.
Cessna 208 has fixed tricycle landing gear, whereas the Cessna 172 also has fixed gear but with a markedly shorter fuselage and low wing.
Cessna 208 has a boxy, slab-sided fuselage with large rectangular cabin windows spaced evenly along its length.
Cessna 208 has a blunt, rounded nose profile distinct from the pointed or tapered noses of the Cessna 525 and Cessna 560.
Cessna 208 has a conventional tail configuration with a single vertical fin and low-mounted horizontal stabilizer, unlike the T-tail of the DHC-6.
Cessna 208 has a taller overall stance than the Cessna 172 due to its higher wing position and longer landing gear struts.
Cessna 208 has a longer fuselage than the Cessna 172, giving it a more elongated utility appearance.
Cessna 208 has no winglets or wingtip devices, distinguishing it visually from modern jets like the Cessna 560.
Cessna 208 has a wide-chord, unswept wing with a constant chord section extending nearly the full span, unlike the tapered wings of the Cessna 525.
Cessna 208 has a single vertical tail fin with a straight leading edge and no dorsal fin extension, unlike the swept dorsal fin of the Cessna 560.
Cessna 208 has a large, upward-hinged cargo door on the left rear fuselage, absent on the Cessna 172 and Cessna 525.
Cessna 208 has a flat, uncurved upper fuselage line running continuously from cockpit to tail, contrasting with the curved upper fuselage of the DHC-6.
Cessna 208 has a noticeably deeper fuselage cross-section than the Cessna 172, contributing to its boxy silhouette.
Cessna 208 has a nose-mounted propeller with three blades, visibly larger in diameter than the two-blade propeller of older Cessna singles like the 172.
Cessna 208 has a ventral fin under the rear fuselage just forward of the tail, not present on the Cessna 172 or Cessna 525.
Cessna 208 has a cockpit windshield composed of multiple flat panes with visible framing, unlike the single-curved windshield of the Cessna 525.
Cessna 208 has main landing gear attached directly to the lower fuselage with simple vertical struts, unlike the wing-mounted gear of the Cessna 560.
Cessna 208 has a short, stubby horizontal stabilizer mounted low on the aft fuselage, contrasting with the high-mounted T-tail of the DHC-6.
Cessna 208 has a wing with pronounced dihedral visible from the front, more exaggerated than the minimal dihedral of the Cessna 172.
Cessna 525: Cessna 525 has a short, compact fuselage with a low passenger window count compared to the longer fuselage and higher window count of the Cessna 560.
Cessna 525 features a low-wing configuration, distinguishing it from the high-wing Beechcraft 1900.
Cessna 525 mounts two turbofan engines on the rear fuselage, unlike the wing-mounted engines of the ERJ 135 and ERJ 145.
Cessna 525 has a T-tail empennage, whereas the Beechcraft 1900 uses a conventional low tailplane.
Cessna 525 exhibits straight to mildly swept wings, in contrast to the more strongly swept wings of the ERJ 135 and ERJ 145.
Cessna 525 has a short, pointed nose with cockpit windows positioned very close to the nose tip, unlike the longer, more rounded nose of the Cessna 560.
Cessna 525 has a small overall size, visibly smaller than the ERJ 145 in both length and height.
Cessna 525 uses a tricycle landing gear configuration with narrow-track main gear, differing from the wider-track main gear of the ERJ 135.
Cessna 525 has a single main cabin door located forward of the wing, whereas the Beechcraft 1900 has a main door aft of the wing.
Cessna 525 has no winglets, unlike the optional winglets found on later Cessna 560 variants.
Cessna 525 has a relatively short fuselage-to-wing chord ratio compared to the elongated fuselage-to-wing chord ratio of the ERJ 145.
Cessna 525 features a smooth, unbroken fuselage contour without a pronounced rear fuselage hump, unlike the stepped rear fuselage profile of the ERJ 135.
Cessna 525 has a narrow, streamlined fuselage cross-section, narrower than the broader fuselage cross-section of the Beechcraft 1900.
Cessna 525 has a single-piece, highly curved windshield with minimal framing, contrasting with the multi-pane, flatter windshield of the Beechcraft 1900.
Cessna 525 has engine nacelles that are closely integrated into the rear fuselage contour, unlike the more protruding nacelles of the ERJ 135.
Cessna 525 has a vertical stabilizer with a straight leading edge and no dorsal fin extension, unlike the ERJ 145’s vertical stabilizer with a prominent dorsal fin.
Cessna 525 has a shallow wing dihedral angle, less pronounced than the higher dihedral seen on the Beechcraft 1900.
Cessna 525 has a short, stubby horizontal stabilizer mounted at the top of the vertical fin, whereas the ERJ 135 has a longer horizontal stabilizer extending well beyond the vertical fin’s sides.
Cessna 525 has a single nose landing gear strut with a narrow wheel track, unlike the dual-strut nose gear of the ERJ 145.
Cessna 525 has a clean, uninterrupted wing-fuselage junction with no fairing bulge, distinguishing it from the noticeable wing root fairing on the Cessna 560.
Cessna 560: Cessna 560 has a low-wing configuration with wings mounted near the bottom of the fuselage.
Cessna 560 features two turbofan engines mounted on the rear fuselage, one on each side.
Cessna 560 uses a T-tail design where the horizontal stabilizer is mounted at the top of the vertical fin.
Cessna 560 has a slender cylindrical fuselage with a pointed nose and moderate length for a midsize business jet.
Cessna 560 has straight wings with minimal sweep compared to the more swept wings of the Embraer Legacy 600.
Cessna 560 has a single main landing gear strut per side, with dual wheels on each main gear.
Cessna 560 has a narrow-body fuselage cross-section smaller in diameter than the Challenger 600.
Cessna 560 has a cockpit with a sharply raked windshield and a distinctively tapered nose profile.
Cessna 560 has two passenger entry doors: one forward on the left side and one aft on the left side.
Cessna 560 has a shorter fuselage than the Challenger 600 but longer than the Cessna 525.
Cessna 560 has engine nacelles that are compact and closely integrated into the rear fuselage contour.
Cessna 560 has a vertical tail fin with a slightly curved leading edge, unlike the straighter fin of the Cessna 525.
Cessna 560 has winglets that are small and upward-canted, differing from the larger blended winglets of the Legacy 600.
Cessna 560 has a nose gear with a single wheel and a relatively short strut compared to the taller nose gear of the Challenger 600.
Cessna 560 has a fuselage taper that begins just behind the wings, creating a more pronounced rear narrowing than the Cessna 525.
Cessna 560 has a rear pressure bulkhead located farther forward than on the Legacy 600, resulting in a shorter aft fuselage section.
Cessna 560 has a wing root fairing that blends smoothly into the fuselage without prominent strakes or pods.
Cessna 560 has a tailcone that slopes downward gently from the T-tail base, less steeply angled than the Legacy 600’s tailcone.
Cessna 560 has a cabin window layout with evenly spaced, rounded rectangular windows and no large overwing exits.
Cessna 560 has a dorsal fin extension that runs forward from the base of the vertical stabilizer, shorter than that on the Challenger 600.
Challenger 600: Challenger 600 has a long, cylindrical fuselage with a tall cabin cross-section relative to the Gulfstream IV's narrower, more tapered fuselage.
Challenger 600 features two turbofan engines mounted on the rear fuselage, one on each side, unlike the Global Express which places its engines further aft and higher on the fuselage.
Challenger 600 has low-mounted swept wings with moderate sweep angle, whereas the Embraer Legacy 600 has wings mounted slightly higher and with greater sweep.
Challenger 600 uses a T-tail configuration with a high horizontal stabilizer atop the vertical fin, in contrast to the Gulfstream V's conventional tail with a lower-mounted horizontal stabilizer.
Challenger 600 has a rounded nose and conventional non-pointed cockpit profile, differing from the sharper, more angular nose of the Gulfstream IV.
Challenger 600 has fewer and larger cabin windows spaced farther apart compared to the denser, smaller window pattern of the Global Express.
Challenger 600 has a relatively short main landing gear strut length, resulting in a lower ground clearance than the Gulfstream V.
Challenger 600 features a single forward passenger door on the left side, positioned just ahead of the wing leading edge, unlike the Legacy 600's door located further aft near the wing trailing edge.
Challenger 600 has a wide, blunt tailcone shape behind the engines, whereas the Global Express has a more tapered, streamlined tailcone.
Challenger 600 exhibits a pronounced vertical fin height relative to fuselage height, exceeding that of the Gulfstream IV.
Challenger 600 has engine nacelles that sit flush against the rear fuselage without prominent pylons, unlike the Gulfstream V's pylon-mounted engines.
Challenger 600 has a straight, uninterrupted dorsal fin line extending from the cockpit to the base of the vertical stabilizer, unlike the curved or stepped dorsal line of the Legacy 600.
Challenger 600 has a wider fuselage diameter than the Gulfstream IV, visible in side-on views as greater lateral bulge amidships.
Challenger 600 has a shorter overall length than the Global Express, evident in reduced distance between nose and tailcone apex.
Challenger 600 has winglets that are small and nearly vertical, contrasting with the large, highly raked winglets of the Gulfstream V.
Challenger 600 has a flat, unbroken underside along the rear fuselage beneath the engines, while the Legacy 600 shows a distinct downward curve under the tailcone.
Challenger 600 has a forward-swept ventral fin at the base of the vertical stabilizer, absent on the Gulfstream IV.
Challenger 600 has a single-piece, smoothly contoured canopy without a distinct windshield frame break, unlike the multi-panel cockpit glazing of the Global Express.
Challenger 600 has main landing gear with dual wheels mounted close together on a single axle, whereas the Gulfstream V uses widely spaced dual-wheel bogies.
Challenger 600 has a distinctive gap between the rear pressure bulkhead and the engine inlets, creating a visible recessed area not found on the Embraer Legacy 600.
DC-10: DC-10 has three engines: two mounted in underwing nacelles and one at the base of the vertical tail fin.
DC-10 features a wide-body fuselage with a tall, slender cylindrical profile typical of 1970s long-haul airliners.
DC-10 has low-mounted swept wings with pronounced dihedral and large winglets absent.
DC-10 uses turbofan engines housed in circular nacelles, with the center engine fed by a distinctive S-duct intake at the fin root.
DC-10 has a conventional vertical tail with a tall, straight leading edge and no raked tip.
DC-10 has a rounded, bulbous nose section with a gently sloping cockpit windscreen and no stepped cockpit profile.
DC-10 has two main landing gear bogies with four wheels each, positioned well aft of the wing trailing edge.
DC-10 has a longer fuselage than the L-1011 but shorter than the MD-11.
DC-10 has wing-mounted engine nacelles set farther outboard compared to the A300B4’s more inboard placement.
DC-10 has a single overwing emergency exit door on each side, unlike the Il-76’s multiple cargo doors.
DC-10 has no winglets or blended winglets, distinguishing it from later MD-11 variants.
DC-10 has a horizontal stabilizer mounted low on the vertical fin, not high-mounted like the Il-76.
DC-10 has a narrow forward fuselage cross-section relative to its wide-body designation, with visible fuselage taper just aft of the cockpit.
DC-10 has a conventional tailcone shape ending in a blunt, rounded fairing—not the upswept tailcone of the MD-11.
DC-10 has main landing gear struts that extend vertically from the fuselage underside, not angled forward like the L-1011’s.
DC-10 has a wing root fairing that smoothly integrates the inboard engine nacelle into the wing’s leading edge.
DC-10 has a cockpit window layout with six forward-facing panes per side, lacking the MD-11’s additional upper window row.
DC-10 has a relatively short rear fuselage section between the wing trailing edge and the tailcone compared to the A300B4.
DC-10 has no dorsal fin extension above the vertical stabilizer, unlike the MD-11’s prominent dorsal fin.
DC-10 has a clean, uninterrupted fuselage belly without external cargo pods or auxiliary power unit humps seen on the Il-76.
DC-3: DC-3 is a low-wing monoplane with wings mounted near the bottom of the fuselage.
DC-3 has two large radial engines mounted on the wings, not on the fuselage or tail.
DC-3 features a conventional tail with a single vertical fin and horizontal stabilizers, unlike the twin-tail layout of the Il-76.
DC-3 uses tailwheel landing gear, giving it a nose-up stance on the ground, unlike the tricycle gear of the DC-6 and C-47 derivatives with modernized undercarriages.
DC-3 has a rounded, bulbous nose profile distinct from the pointed or flattened noses of the An-12 and Il-76.
DC-3 has straight wings with rounded tips, lacking the swept wings seen on jet-era transports like the Il-76.
DC-3 has a relatively short and stout fuselage compared to the longer, more slender fuselage of the DC-6.
DC-3 has no jet intakes or exhausts anywhere on the airframe, distinguishing it from turbofan-powered variants like the Il-76.
DC-3 has a cylindrical fuselage cross-section with gentle tapering, unlike the boxier mid-fuselage section of the An-12.
DC-3 has radial engine nacelles that protrude prominently forward of the wing leading edge, unlike the smoother, more integrated nacelles of the C-47’s later production variants.
DC-3 has a single vertical stabilizer with a curved trailing edge, whereas the Il-76 has a tall, angular double-fin configuration.
DC-3 has a cockpit canopy with multiple framed windows forming a stepped, rounded profile, unlike the continuous bubble canopy of some An-12 variants.
DC-3 has a narrow fuselage diameter that appears proportionally smaller than the wider, more voluminous fuselage of the Il-76.
DC-3 has wing-mounted engines positioned well ahead of the wing’s quarter-chord line, creating a distinctive forward-hanging nacelle appearance absent in the rear-mounted engines of the An-12.

DC-3 has a tailwheel configuration where the main wheels are forward of the center of gravity, resulting in a visibly tilted-up nose, unlike the level stance of tricycle-gear C-47s in postwar configurations.
DC-3 has a gently sloping dorsal spine that tapers smoothly into the tail, unlike the abrupt, squared-off dorsal hump of the Il-76.
DC-3 has a simple, unbroken wing leading edge with no winglets or fillets, distinguishing it from modernized or retrofitted C-47 variants with added aerodynamic fairings.
DC-3 has a short, stubby fuselage relative to its wingspan, giving it a compact, balanced silhouette unlike the elongated proportions of the DC-6.
DC-3 has a single, centrally located main cabin door on the left side, typically without the multiple cargo doors or clamshell rear ramps found on the C-47 and Il-76.
DC-3 has a classic pre-jet airliner shape defined by its rounded contours, lack of sharp angles, and absence of high-mounted T-tails or cruciform tails seen on later transports.
DC-6: DC-6 has a low-mounted wing with moderate taper and no sweep, unlike the swept wings of the DC-8 and L-1011.
DC-6 features four piston-prop engines mounted in nacelles under the wings, whereas the DC-3 has only two and the DC-8 has four jet engines.
DC-6 has radial-engine nacelles with large-diameter propeller discs, distinguishing it from the slender jet nacelles of the DC-8 and L-1011.
DC-6 has a rounded, pressurized fuselage cross-section typical of mid-century airliners, unlike the flatter-sided C-47 or the narrower DC-3 fuselage.
DC-6 has a conventional tail configuration with a single vertical fin and horizontal stabilizers mounted on the fuselage, not a T-tail like the L-1011.
DC-6 has tricycle landing gear with main gear retracting inward into the wing, unlike the tailwheel configuration of the DC-3 and C-47.
DC-6 has a longer fuselage than the DC-3 and C-47, giving it a more stretched appearance despite sharing the same basic wing and tail layout.
DC-6 has a cockpit with a distinctively curved, multi-pane windshield and a pronounced nose contour, less blunt than the DC-8’s nose and more rounded than the C-47’s.
DC-6 has passenger doors positioned forward of the wing leading edge, whereas the C-47 typically has its main door aft of the wing and the DC-3 often has a single door mid-fuselage.
DC-6 has a wider fuselage diameter than the DC-3, visible in the fuller, more cylindrical profile when viewed from front or rear.
DC-6 has engine nacelles that extend well ahead of the wing’s leading edge, unlike the more compact, flush-mounted nacelles of later jetliners.
DC-6 has a straight, unbroken dorsal spine running from cockpit to tail, lacking the hump or raised section seen on the L-1011.
DC-6 has a ventral fin beneath the rear fuselage just forward of the tail, absent on the DC-3 and C-47.
DC-6 has a taller main landing gear strut than the DC-3, resulting in greater ground clearance and a more upright stance.
DC-6 has a wing with noticeable dihedral and a clean, unswept planform, contrasting sharply with the high-aspect-ratio, highly tapered wings of the L-1011.
DC-6 has a tailcone that tapers smoothly to a point without the bulbous APU exhaust fairing found on the DC-8.
DC-6 has a nose gear with a single wheel and a narrow fork, unlike the dual-wheel nose gear of the DC-8 and L-1011.
DC-6 has wingtips that are squared-off or slightly rounded, not clipped or fitted with winglets like modern jets or the swept-wing DC-8.
DC-6 has a cabin window layout with evenly spaced, oval-shaped windows of consistent size, differing from the smaller, more numerous windows of the DC-3 and the larger, fewer windows of the DC-8.
DC-6 has a tailplane with marked anhedral (downward angle), a subtle but consistent feature not shared by the level or upward-angled tailplanes of the DC-8 or L-1011.
DC-8: DC-8 has a long, slender narrow-body fuselage distinct from the wider fuselages of the DC-10 and MD-11.
DC-8 features four podded turbofan engines mounted under the wings, two per wing, unlike the three-engine layout of the DC-10 and MD-11.
DC-8 has low-mounted swept wings, whereas the 727-200 has a high-mounted wing.
DC-8 possesses a conventional tail with a single vertical fin and low horizontal stabilizer, differing from the T-tail of the 727-200.
DC-8 exhibits a long pointed nose profile, more elongated than the shorter, blunter nose of the 707-320.
DC-8 has a relatively narrow fuselage cross-section compared to the widebody DC-10 and MD-11.
DC-8 uses podded jet engines with circular nacelles, unlike the blended engine pods sometimes seen on later MD-11 variants.
DC-8 has main landing gear with four-wheel bogies arranged in a tandem configuration under the fuselage, unlike the 707-320’s dual-wheel main gear.
DC-8 features a straight, unbroken fuselage side contour without the pronounced rear fuselage taper of the 727-200.
DC-8 has a cockpit window arrangement with a distinctive five-pane forward windshield and angled side windows, differing from the 707-320’s six-pane windshield.
DC-8 has passenger doors positioned only along the left side of the forward and mid-fuselage, with no rear door like the 727-200.
DC-8 lacks the dorsal fin extension found on the 707-320’s vertical stabilizer.
DC-8 has wing-mounted engine pylons that extend farther forward relative to the leading edge than those on the 707-320.
DC-8 has a longer fuselage than the 727-200, with greater overall length visible between nose and tail.
DC-8 features a ventral fin beneath the rear fuselage, absent on the 727-200.
DC-8 has a narrower wing chord and thinner airfoil appearance compared to the broader, more robust wings of the DC-10.
DC-8 has no winglets or wingtip devices, distinguishing it from some later 707-320B/C variants retrofitted with them.
DC-8 has a smooth, uninterrupted fuselage roofline without the raised cockpit hump of the 727-200.
DC-8 has a tailcone that tapers gradually to a fine point, unlike the more blunt, rounded tailcone of the MD-11.
DC-8 has a single, continuous canopy line over the cockpit without the stepped or segmented glazing seen on the 707-320.
DC-9-30: DC-9-30 has a shorter fuselage than the MD-80.
DC-9-30 features twin rear-mounted turbofan engines, unlike the underwing-mounted engines of the Boeing 717.
DC-9-30 has a T-tail configuration with the horizontal stabilizer mounted high on the vertical fin.
DC-9-30 has low-mounted swept wings with no engine nacelles attached beneath them.
DC-9-30 has a slender narrow-body fuselage with a single-aisle cross-section, narrower than the MD-90's fuselage.
DC-9-30 has main landing gear housed in streamlined pods at the wing root-fuselage junction, not in large underwing fairings.
DC-30 has a shorter nose and more compact cockpit profile compared to the MD-87.
DC-9-30 has a clean wing root without winglets or wingtip devices, unlike later MD-90 variants.
DC-9-30 has a conventional tailcone tapering smoothly to a point, whereas the MD-80 series has a slightly blunter tailcone.
DC-9-30 has two passenger doors on the left side forward of the wing and one aft of the wing, differing from the MD-90’s four forward doors.
DC-9-30 has a shorter overall length than the MD-90.
DC-9-30 has a less pronounced wing sweep angle than the Boeing 717.
DC-9-30 has no auxiliary power unit (APU) inlet visible on the upper rear fuselage, unlike the MD-80 series.
DC-9-30 has a narrower vertical fin base relative to fuselage width compared to the MD-90.
DC-9-30 has a simpler, unfaired rear fuselage contour behind the engines, lacking the MD-80’s extended tailcone fairing.
DC-9-30 has a straighter, less curved upper fuselage line from cockpit to tail than the MD-90.
DC-9-30 has smaller-diameter engines mounted closer together on the rear fuselage than the MD-80.
DC-9-30 has a shorter distance between the trailing edge of the wing and the leading edge of the horizontal stabilizer than the MD-90.
DC-9-30 has a more rounded cockpit window arrangement with fewer panes than the MD-87’s angular, multi-pane design.
DC-9-30 has a narrower chord vertical stabilizer than the Boeing 717.
DH-82: DH-82 has two stacked wings connected by visible interplane struts and bracing wires.
DH-82 features a single nose-mounted piston engine with an exposed propeller.
DH-82 has a slender, fabric-covered fuselage significantly narrower than the Cessna 172's tubular metal fuselage.
DH-82 uses fixed tailwheel landing gear, unlike the tricycle gear of the Cessna 172 and DR-400.
DH-82 has a conventional tail with a low-mounted horizontal stabilizer, contrasting with the Spitfire's cantilever monoplane tail mounted higher on the fuselage.
DH-82 lacks wing sweep entirely, while the Spitfire has distinctly swept-back wings.
DH-82 has tandem two-seat cockpit windows aligned vertically along the fuselage, unlike the side-by-side windows of the DR-400.
DH-82 has no cabin doors—only small hinged cockpit access panels—unlike the large sliding or hinged cabin doors of the DHC-1.
DH-82’s upper wing is noticeably longer in span than its lower wing, whereas the DHC-1 has equal-span wings.
DH-82 has prominent external bracing wires running from the upper wing to the lower fuselage, absent on the all-metal monoplane Cessna 172.
DH-82’s nose section is short and blunt with a radial-style engine cowling, unlike the elongated, pointed nose of the Spitfire.
DH-82 has a deeply tapered rudder extending well below the fuselage, unlike the shorter, more rectangular rudder of the DR-400.
DH-82’s wings are staggered with the upper wing positioned forward of the lower wing, unlike the aligned wings of the Cessna 172.
DH-82 has no winglets or wingtip devices, distinguishing it from modern variants like the DHC-1 which sometimes feature them.
DH-82’s fuselage tapers sharply aft of the cockpit, whereas the DR-400 maintains a more cylindrical cross-section rearward.
DH-82 has an open-style cockpit without a continuous canopy, unlike the fully enclosed bubble canopy of the Spitfire.
DH-82’s main landing gear legs are simple, vertical steel tubes with rubber cord suspension, unlike the oleo-strut gear of the Cessna 172.
DH-82 has a narrow-chord horizontal stabilizer mounted low on the fuselage, unlike the wider, mid-fuselage stabilizer of the DHC-1.
DH-82’s wing struts are thick, streamlined steel tubes with external bracing wires, unlike the clean, strutless wing of the DR-400.
DH-82 has a single, uncowled exhaust stack emerging from the upper engine cylinder bank, unlike the multiple evenly spaced exhaust stubs of the Spitfire’s inline engine.
DHC-1: DHC-1 has a tailwheel landing gear configuration, unlike the tricycle gear of the Cessna 172 and PA-28.
DHC-1 features low-mounted straight wings with rounded tips, whereas the DH-82 has slightly tapered wings with squared tips.
DHC-1 has a slender tandem two-seat canopy extending nearly the full length of the fuselage, unlike the shorter, more bulbous canopy of the DHC-6.
DHC-1 possesses a smooth all-metal fuselage with a pointed nose spinner, in contrast to the blunt, non-spinnner nose of the PA-28.
DHC-1 has a conventional tail with a single vertical fin and low-mounted horizontal stabilizers, differing from the high-mounted T-tail of the DHC-6.
DHC-1 is a single-engine propeller aircraft with the engine mounted in the nose, unlike the twin-engine layout of the DHC-6.
DHC-1 has a short, compact fuselage proportionally shorter than the DH-82’s longer, deeper fuselage.
DHC-1 exhibits a narrow chord wing relative to fuselage width, while the Cessna 172 has a broader chord wing.
DHC-1 uses a piston engine driving a two-blade propeller, whereas the DHC-6 uses turboprop engines with three- or four-blade propellers.
DHC-1 has no winglets or wingtip devices, unlike some modernized PA-28 variants that feature winglets.
DHC-1 has a rounded, streamlined fuselage cross-section tapering smoothly to the tail, unlike the more angular rear fuselage of the DH-82.
DHC-1 features a single-piece, rear-hinged canopy over both cockpits, whereas the Cessna 172 has separate side-hinged doors.
DHC-1 has a very short nose section ahead of the cockpit, significantly shorter than the extended nose of the DH-82.
DHC-1 has no external baggage door on the fuselage, unlike the prominent aft baggage door found on the PA-28.
DHC-1 has a narrow-track tailwheel gear with widely splayed main gear struts, unlike the narrow-track tricycle gear of the Cessna 172.
DHC-1 displays a clean, uncluttered wing leading edge with no flaps visible in retracted position, unlike the DH-82’s prominent split flaps.
DHC-1 has a shallow dorsal ridge running along the upper fuselage spine from cockpit to tail, absent on the smoother PA-28 upper fuselage.
DHC-1 has a small, circular engine cowling with minimal frontal area, contrasting with the larger-diameter cowling of the DH-82’s de Havilland Gipsy Major.
DHC-1 has a vertical tail fin with a gently curved leading edge and no dorsal fillet, unlike the DH-82’s fin with a distinct dorsal extension.
DHC-1 has a low-wing configuration where the wing root joins the fuselage at the bottom third of its height, whereas the DHC-6 wing root attaches near mid-fuselage.
DHC-6: DHC-6 has a short, boxy fuselage with a blunt forward profile and relatively short nose compared to the longer, more tapered fuselage of the DHC-8-100.
DHC-6 features a high-mounted straight wing, unlike the low-mounted slightly swept wing of the ATR-42.
DHC-6 mounts two turboprop engines directly under the wings on pylons, whereas the Saab 340 mounts its engines on the rear fuselage.
DHC-6 has fixed tricycle landing gear with exposed wheels and no gear doors, in contrast to the retractable gear with full wheel wells of the DHC-8-300.
DHC-6 displays large rectangular cabin windows spaced closely along a short fuselage, unlike the smaller, more widely spaced oval windows of the ATR-42.
DHC-6 has a tall, narrow vertical tail with a conventional low-mounted horizontal stabilizer, differing from the T-tail configuration of the Saab 340.
DHC-6 has a rugged, utilitarian stance with pronounced ground clearance and short main gear legs, unlike the lower-slung commuter posture of the DHC-8-100.
DHC-6 features a flat, unfaired engine nacelle underside with visible propeller spinners, unlike the streamlined, faired nacelles of the DHC-8 series.
DHC-6 has a straight, unswept wing with no dihedral or anhedral visible in standard views, whereas the DHC-8-300 wing exhibits noticeable dihedral.
DHC-6 has a single large forward passenger door on the left side near the cockpit, unlike the dual overwing exits and rear airstair of the ATR-42.
DHC-6 has a wide-chord, blunt-nosed cockpit glazing with minimal curvature, contrasting with the sharply raked, highly curved windshield of the DHC-8-100.
DHC-6 has no winglets or wingtip devices, while the DHC-8-300 often features small blended winglets.
DHC-6 has a short, vertically oriented dorsal fin extension atop the vertical stabilizer, absent on the smoother trailing edge of the ATR-42’s fin.
DHC-6 has a simple, uncluttered wing leading edge with no slats or Krueger flaps visible, unlike the complex high-lift devices on the DHC-8-300 wing.
DHC-6 has a fuselage cross-section that appears nearly square in side profile due to its boxy construction, whereas the Saab 340 fuselage is distinctly oval and narrower in proportion.
DHC-6 has a short, stubby tailcone ending abruptly behind the horizontal stabilizer, unlike the elongated, tapered tailcone of the DHC-8-100.
DHC-6 has a prominent, flat-panel cargo door on the right rear fuselage, a feature not present on the passenger-only configured DHC-8 variants.
DHC-6 has a straight, uninterrupted upper fuselage line from nose to tail without the pronounced hump or curvature seen on the ATR-42’s roofline.
DHC-6 has main landing gear struts mounted directly to the fuselage underside with no wing fairings, unlike the wing-root-mounted gear with large fairings on the Saab 340.
DHC-6 has a high-wing configuration where the wing root joins the top of the fuselage, clearly separating it from the mid-wing placement of the DHC-8-300.
DHC-8-100: DHC-8-100 has a shorter fuselage than the DHC-8-300.
DHC-8-100 features a high-mounted straight wing, unlike the low-mounted swept wings of the ATR-42 and ATR-72.
DHC-8-100 has two turboprop engines mounted in underslung nacelles beneath the wings.
DHC-8-100 displays a conventional tail with a tall vertical fin and low-mounted horizontal stabilizers, contrasting with the T-tail of the Saab 340.
DHC-8-100 has a pointed nose profile distinct from the more rounded nose of the ATR-42.
DHC-8-100 uses tricycle landing gear with main wheels retracting into streamlined fairings adjacent to the engine nacelles.
DHC-8-100 has a long, slim cylindrical fuselage shape unlike the slightly stockier fuselage cross-section of the ATR-72.
DHC-8-100 has a single row of evenly spaced rectangular cabin windows along the fuselage, differing from the staggered or double-row window layouts on some Saab 340 variants.
DHC-8-100 has no winglets or wingtip devices, unlike later-production ATR-72s that sometimes feature winglets.
DHC-8-100 has engine nacelles that extend forward of the leading edge of the wing, whereas ATR-42 nacelles are more closely aligned with the wing's leading edge.
DHC-8-100 has a cockpit windshield with a pronounced forward rake and three distinct pane divisions, unlike the flatter, four-pane layout of the ATR-42.
DHC-8-100 has a main passenger door located just aft of the wing trailing edge, while the Saab 340 places its main door significantly farther aft.
DHC-8-100 has a relatively narrow fuselage diameter compared to the ATR-72, visible in side-on profile as reduced girth.
DHC-8-100 has a vertical stabilizer with a straight leading edge and no dorsal fin extension, unlike the curved leading edge and prominent dorsal fin on many ATR-72s.
DHC-8-100 has wing-mounted engines positioned closer to the fuselage than those on the ATR-42, resulting in shorter nacelle-to-fuselage gaps.
DHC-8-100 has a horizontal stabilizer mounted low on the vertical fin, not at the top like the T-tail configuration of the Saab 340.
DHC-8-100 has a smooth, uninterrupted fuselage contour without the pronounced rear fuselage step found on some ATR-42 variants.
DHC-8-100 has a nose gear with a single wheel and a narrow track, contrasting with the wider-track dual-wheel nose gear on later ATR-72 models.
DHC-8-100 has a wing root that blends smoothly into the fuselage with minimal filleting, unlike the more bulbous wing-root fairings on the ATR-72.
DHC-8-100 has a tailcone that tapers gradually to a fine point, whereas the Saab 340 tailcone ends more abruptly with a flattened tip.
DHC-8-300: DHC-8-300 has a high-mounted straight wing positioned well above the fuselage centerline.
DHC-8-300 features two turboprop engines, each mounted in a nacelle beneath the wing.
DHC-8-300 has a T-tail configuration with the horizontal stabilizer mounted atop the vertical fin.
DHC-8-300 possesses a slender cylindrical fuselage without a bulged cross-section or fuselage hump.
DHC-8-300 uses tricycle landing gear with main wheels retracting into streamlined pods attached near the fuselage underside.
DHC-8-300 has large rectangular cabin windows arranged in a consistent commuter-airliner layout with uniform spacing.
DHC-8-300 has a conventional non-tapered nose section ending in a rounded cockpit glazing profile.
DHC-8-300 has a straight wing with no sweep, distinguishing it from the slightly swept wings of the ATR-72.
DHC-8-300 has a longer fuselage than the DHC-8-100 but shorter than the DHC-8-400.
DHC-8-300 has engine nacelles suspended below the wing rather than integrated into the wing leading edge like the Saab 340.
DHC-8-300 has a taller vertical fin relative to fuselage height compared to the ATR-42.
DHC-8-300 has a single main passenger door on the left side forward of the wing, unlike the ATR-72’s dual forward and aft doors.
DHC-8-300 has a narrower fuselage diameter than the ATR-72, visible in cross-sectional proportion.
DHC-8-300 has wing-mounted engines placed farther outboard than those on the Saab 340.
DHC-8-300 has a more pronounced dorsal fin extension at the base of the vertical stabilizer than the ATR-42.
DHC-8-300 has a straight, unbroken fuselage top line without the raised roof section seen on the ATR-72.
DHC-8-300 has landing gear struts that extend vertically downward from the fuselage pods, not angled inward like some Saab 340 configurations.
DHC-8-300 has a cockpit windshield with a flatter upper curvature compared to the more domed windshield of the ATR-42.
DHC-8-300 has a shorter nose section ahead of the cockpit windows than the ATR-72.
DHC-8-300 has a wing chord that remains constant along its span, unlike the tapered wing of the Saab 340.
DR-400: DR-400 is a small low-wing monoplane, unlike the high-wing Cessna 172.
DR-400 has fixed tricycle landing gear, whereas the DHC-1 has conventional tailwheel landing gear.
DR-400 features a bubble-style cockpit canopy with extensive glazing, contrasting with the flatter, more angular canopy of the PA-28.
DR-400 has a slender light-aircraft fuselage proportionally shorter than the SR-20's fuselage.
DR-400 mounts a single piston engine in the nose driving a two- or three-blade propeller, unlike the turbine-powered DHC-1.
DR-400 exhibits a conventional tail with a single vertical fin and low-mounted horizontal stabilizer, differing from the T-tail of the SR-20.
DR-400 has a rounded, smoothly tapered nose profile distinct from the more blunt, squared-off nose of the PA-28.
DR-400’s wing is mounted low on the fuselage, while the Cessna 172’s wing is mounted high.
DR-400’s wing has no sweep and minimal dihedral, unlike the noticeably swept wingtips of the SR-20.
DR-400 has a narrow-chord wing with straight leading and trailing edges, contrasting with the tapered, elliptical wing planform of the DHC-1.
DR-400’s fuselage tapers gradually to a fine rear end, whereas the PA-28’s fuselage ends more abruptly at the tailcone.
DR-400 features a single-piece, forward-hinged canopy that extends over both cockpits, unlike the side-hinged doors of the Cessna 172.
DR-400’s vertical stabilizer is narrower and less tall relative to fuselage height than the PA-28’s.
DR-400 has a smooth, uninterrupted fuselage side contour without prominent strakes or fairings, unlike the SR-20’s rear fuselage strake.
DR-400’s main landing gear legs are vertically oriented and unfaired, whereas the Cessna 172’s gear legs tilt slightly aft.
DR-400’s horizontal stabilizer is mounted low on the vertical fin, not at the top like the SR-20’s T-tail.
DR-400’s cockpit glazing wraps farther forward around the nose than the PA-28’s, creating a more enclosed, rounded frontal view.
DR-400’s wing root blends smoothly into the fuselage with minimal step or gap, unlike the pronounced wing-fuselage junction on the DHC-1.
DR-400’s propeller hub is relatively small and centered on a shallow, rounded spinner, contrasting with the larger, more elongated spinner of the PA-28.
DR-400’s overall silhouette is more compact and lightweight in appearance than the broader, heavier-looking SR-20.
Dornier 328: Dornier 328 has a short, compact fuselage distinctly shorter than the Saab 340.
Dornier 328 features a high-mounted straight wing, unlike the low-mounted wing of the Beechcraft 1900.
Dornier 328 mounts one turboprop engine under each wing, whereas the EMB-120 has engines mounted on the rear fuselage.
Dornier 328 uses turboprop engines with visible propellers, distinguishing it from jet-powered regional aircraft like the CRJ-200.
Dornier 328 has a T-tail configuration with the horizontal stabilizer mounted high on the vertical fin, unlike the conventional tail of the DHC-8-100.
Dornier 328 has a pointed, streamlined nose profile, more tapered than the blunt nose of the Saab 340.
Dornier 328 has a relatively sleek, slender fuselage cross-section compared to the boxier fuselage of the Beechcraft 1900.
Dornier 328 features main landing gear positioned under the wing root area, not under the mid-fuselage like the EMB-120.
Dornier 328 has a narrow-track tricycle landing gear with closely spaced main wheels, unlike the wider stance of the DHC-8-100.
Dornier 328 has a single forward passenger door located just ahead of the wing leading edge, whereas the Saab 340 places its forward door further aft.
Dornier 328 has no overwing emergency exits, distinguishing it from the Beechcraft 1900 which features two overwing exits.
Dornier 328 has a smooth, uninterrupted fuselage contour without a pronounced rear fuselage hump, unlike the EMB-120’s raised aft section.
Dornier 328 has a straight, un-swept wing with minimal dihedral, contrasting with the noticeable dihedral of the DHC-8-100’s wing.
Dornier 328 has a relatively long, slender tailfin extending well above the T-tail junction, taller than the Saab 340’s vertical stabilizer.
Dornier 328 has a cockpit windscreen with a distinctive five-panel layout and a pronounced downward slope, unlike the flatter, three-panel windscreen of the Beechcraft 1900.
Dornier 328 has a clean wing-fuselage junction with no fairing or bulge, in contrast to the prominent wing-root fairing on the EMB-120.
Dornier 328 has a small, compact tailcone tapering sharply behind the T-tail, shorter than the elongated tailcone of the DHC-8-100.
Dornier 328 has a narrow, cylindrical fuselage diameter that remains consistent along most of its length, unlike the slightly widened mid-fuselage of the Saab 340.
Dornier 328 has engine nacelles that sit flush beneath the wings with minimal protrusion, whereas the Beechcraft 1900’s nacelles extend noticeably forward of the wing leading edge.
Dornier 328 has a single rear service door located just forward of the tailcone, differing from the EMB-120’s rear door placement at the very end of the fuselage.
E-170: E-170 has a shorter fuselage than the E-190 and E-195.
E-170 features low-mounted swept wings with small blended wingtip fences, unlike the larger winglets on CRJ-900.
E-170 has twin underwing turbofan engines mounted closer to the fuselage than those on the CRJ-700.
E-170 displays a conventional tail with a single vertical fin and low-set horizontal stabilizers, contrasting with the T-tail of the CRJ family.
E-170 has a round-nosed fuselage with a clean cylindrical cross-section, differing from the more tapered nose of the CRJ-700.
E-170 has main landing gear that retracts into fairings near the wing root rather than into large pods like the CRJ-900.
E-170 has a stubbier overall proportion compared to the longer, leaner CRJ-700.
E-170 has a taller cabin cross-section than the CRJ-700, visible in side profile as greater fuselage height relative to length.
E-170 has no winglets—only small blended wingtip fences—unlike the prominent winglets on the E-195.
E-170 has a shorter forward fuselage ahead of the wing than the E-190, making the cockpit appear more compact in side view.
E-170 has two passenger doors on the left side forward of the wing and one aft of the wing, whereas the CRJ-900 has two forward and two aft.
E-170 has a lower wing position relative to the fuselage centerline than the higher-mounted wings of the CRJ-700.
E-170 has a less-swept wing leading edge compared to the more aggressively swept wings of the CRJ-900.
E-170 has a single vertical stabilizer with a rounded top, unlike the squared-off fin tip sometimes seen on older CRJ variants.
E-170 has a smoother, more continuous fuselage contour without the pronounced rear taper of the CRJ-700.
E-170 has engine nacelles that sit closer to the fuselage underside, creating a narrower gap than on the E-195.
E-170 has a shorter distance between the trailing edge of the wing and the leading edge of the horizontal stabilizer than the E-190.
E-170 has a wider fuselage diameter than the CRJ-700, evident in the fuller, less slender side profile.
E-170 has a cockpit windshield with a shallower rake angle than the steeper, more angular windshield of the CRJ-900.
E-170 has a shorter rear fuselage section behind the wing than the E-195, resulting in a more compact tailcone.
E-190: E-190 has a fuselage length intermediate between the shorter E-170 and the longer E-195.
E-190 features twin underwing turbofan engines mounted close to the fuselage, distinguishing it from the overwing engines of the An-148.
E-190 has low-mounted swept wings with a clean trailing edge, unlike the CRJ-900’s more complex winglet-integrated trailing edge.
E-190 displays a conventional tail with a swept vertical fin and low-set horizontal stabilizers, contrasting with the Fokker 100’s T-tail configuration.
E-190 possesses a slender narrow-body fuselage visibly smaller in diameter than mainline single-aisle jets like the A320.
E-190 has a rounded nose profile with large cockpit windows typical of modern regional jets, differing from the sharper, more angular nose of the CRJ-900.
E-190 exhibits short-to-medium landing gear giving it a relatively low stance on the ground, unlike the taller gear of the Fokker 100.
E-190 has two turbofan engines, ruling out turboprop configurations like those on the ATR 72.
E-190 features a wing sweep angle consistent across the E-Jet family, shallower than the more aggressively swept wings of the Boeing 737 NG.
E-190 has a single main passenger door forward of the wing and a second main door aft of the wing, differing from the CRJ-900’s single main door ahead of the wing.
E-190’s fuselage is longer than the E-170’s but shorter than the E-195’s, visible in side-profile proportion comparisons.
E-190 has no winglets, distinguishing it from the blended winglets of the later E-190-E2.
E-190’s horizontal stabilizers are mounted low on the vertical fin, unlike the high-mounted stabilizers of the Fokker 100.
E-190’s engine nacelles are circular and unfluted, contrasting with the flattened, fluted nacelles of the CRJ-900.
E-190 has a smooth, uninterrupted fuselage contour without the pronounced rear fuselage taper seen on the Fokker 100.
E-190’s cockpit windows form a continuous curved arc across the nose, unlike the segmented, flatter glazing of the CRJ-900.
E-190’s wing root blends smoothly into the fuselage with minimal step or gap, unlike the more pronounced wing-fuselage junction on the older Fokker 100.
E-190’s main landing gear retracts inward into the fuselage with dual wheels, differing from the single-wheel main gear of the E-170.
E-190’s vertical fin has a straight leading edge and moderate sweep, less raked than the sharply swept fin of the A320.
E-190’s cabin windows are evenly spaced and uniformly sized along the fuselage, unlike the irregular spacing and varying sizes on the Fokker 100.
E-195: E-195 has a longer fuselage than the E-170 and E-190 within the same Embraer E-Jet family.
E-195 features twin underwing turbofan engines mounted close to the fuselage, unlike the CRJ-900's more outward-mounted engines.
E-195 has low-mounted swept wings with small blended winglets, whereas the Fokker 100 has unswept wings and no winglets.
E-195 uses conventional tail configuration with a single vertical fin and no T-tail, distinguishing it from the Fokker 100's T-tail.
E-195 has a rounded nose and large cockpit windshield, contrasting with the CRJ-900's more pointed nose and smaller windshield.
E-195 has main landing gear that retracts into fairings at the wing root and fuselage junction, not into fuselage-mounted pods like the CRJ-900.
E-195 has a narrow-body fuselage proportionally longer and fuller than the E-170 but shorter and less elongated than typical mainline jets like the A320.
E-195 has wing sweep angled noticeably more than the Fokker 100’s nearly straight wings.
E-195 has two turbofan engines, not the three engines of the Fokker 100 or the two turboprops of the ATR 72.
E-195 has a clean, streamlined fuselage contour without the pronounced rear taper seen on the CRJ-900.
E-195 has a single vertical stabilizer with a raked trailing edge, unlike the CRJ-900’s more upright and squared-off fin.
E-195 has a fuselage cross-section that appears wider relative to length compared to the pencil-thin CRJ-900.
E-195 has wingtip devices that appear as small blended winglets from most angles, whereas the E-170 and E-190 may show raked wingtips depending on subvariant.
E-195 has a cockpit canopy with a continuous curved upper surface, unlike the stepped or segmented glazing of older regional jets like the Fokker 100.
E-195 has engine nacelles positioned closer to the fuselage than those on the CRJ-900, giving tighter wing-root integration.
E-195 has a tailplane mounted on the lower half of the vertical fin, not at the top like the T-tail of the Fokker 100.
E-195 has a forward passenger door located just ahead of the wing leading edge, whereas the CRJ-900 places its forward door further forward relative to wing position.
E-195 has a fuselage that tapers gradually toward the rear without the abrupt narrowing seen on the Fokker 100.
E-195 has wing roots that blend smoothly into the fuselage with minimal step or gap, unlike the more pronounced junction on the CRJ-900.
E-195 has a medium-length narrow-body airframe distinctly longer than the E-170 but visibly shorter than the A320, placing it in the upper tier of regional jet sizing.
EMB-120: EMB-120 has a slender, narrow fuselage proportionally shorter than the DHC-8-300.
EMB-120 features low-mounted wings with no wing sweep, unlike the slightly swept wings of the Saab 340.
EMB-120 is powered by two turboprop engines mounted directly under the wings in streamlined nacelles.
EMB-120 has a conventional tail configuration with a single vertical fin and low-set horizontal stabilizers, distinct from the T-tail of the Beechcraft 1900.
EMB-120 exhibits a pointed, streamlined nose section with a gently curved cockpit glazing profile.
EMB-120 has main landing gear that retracts fully into fairings beneath the engine nacelles, preserving a clean wing underside silhouette.
EMB-120 has a single forward passenger door on the left side, positioned just ahead of the wing leading edge.
EMB-120 has a relatively short fuselage compared to the DHC-8-100, with fewer windows between the cockpit and wing.
EMB-120 displays twin turboprop engines with three-blade propellers, visually smaller in diameter than those on the DHC-8 series.

Spitfire’s vertical stabilizer is relatively tall and narrow compared to the broader, swept vertical fin of the Eurofighter Typhoon.
Spitfire’s main landing gear retracts outward into the wings, while the Hawk T1’s main gear retracts inward toward the fuselage.
Spitfire has a short, stubby tailcone behind the horizontal stabilizers, unlike the elongated rear fuselage of the DHC-1.
Spitfire’s engine cowling is smooth and tightly fitted around a radial or inline piston engine, not bulging like the DH-82’s radial engine housing.
Spitfire’s fuselage tapers sharply aft of the cockpit, whereas the DHC-1’s fuselage maintains a more cylindrical cross-section rearward.
Spitfire has no dorsal fin extension above the fuselage, unlike the Hawk T1 which features a distinct dorsal strake.
Spitfire’s wing chord is widest near the fuselage and tapers smoothly outward, differing from the DH-82’s more uniform chord and squared-off wingtips.
Tornado: Tornado has variable-sweep wings that pivot from fully extended forward to sharply swept back positions, unlike the fixed wings of the Eurofighter Typhoon.
Tornado features two side-by-side exhaust nozzles at the rear fuselage, whereas the F-16A/B has a single centered exhaust.
Tornado possesses a shoulder-mounted wing configuration, in contrast to the mid-wing placement of the F/A-18.
Tornado displays a long, slender fuselage with a pronounced taper toward the tail, longer and more elongated than the compact fuselage of the Hawk T1.
Tornado has a single vertical tail fin, differing from the twin vertical fins of the F/A-18.
Tornado exhibits low-mounted horizontal tailplanes attached directly to the rear fuselage, unlike the high-mounted or all-moving tails of the Eurofighter Typhoon.
Tornado shows a long, stepped cockpit canopy accommodating two crew members in tandem, whereas the F-16A/B has a single-seat bubble canopy.
Tornado has a deep, wide engine bay housing two turbofan engines, visually distinct from the narrower single-engine bay of the F-16A/B.
Tornado features a blunt, rounded nose profile with a prominent radar dome, contrasting with the pointed, slender nose of the Eurofighter Typhoon.
Tornado displays a wide-track main landing gear with dual wheels per strut, unlike the narrow-track single-wheel main gear of the Hawk T1.
Tornado has a continuous, unbroken fuselage contour from nose to tail without pronounced humps or bulges, unlike the raised spine and dorsal hump of the F/A-18.
Tornado shows wing root extensions blending smoothly into the fuselage, whereas the Eurofighter Typhoon has sharp, angular wing-fuselage junctions.
Tornado possesses a relatively short, stubby intake duct located beneath the cockpit, unlike the large, rectangular intakes of the F/A-18.
Tornado has a straight, non-canted vertical tail fin, while the Eurofighter Typhoon’s fin is noticeably canted outward.
Tornado features a wide, flat underside on the rear fuselage between the engines, contrasting with the deeply recessed, narrow ventral area of the F-16A/B.
Tornado displays a prominent dorsal spine running along the upper fuselage centerline behind the cockpit, absent on the Hawk T1.
Tornado has a wide, shallow fuselage cross-section visible in three-quarter views, whereas the F-16A/B appears deeper and narrower vertically.
Tornado shows a distinct gap between the trailing edge of the wing and the leading edge of the horizontal tailplane, unlike the overlapping or flush arrangement seen on the Eurofighter Typhoon.
Tornado features a long, uninterrupted canopy frame with multiple transverse structural bars, unlike the frameless or minimally framed bubble canopy of the F-16A/B.
Tornado has a rear fuselage that tapers gradually and symmetrically to the exhausts, unlike the abrupt, squared-off rear end of the Hawk T1.
Tu-134: Tu-134 has two turbofan engines mounted on the rear fuselage, not under the wings like the DC-9-30 or MD-80.
Tu-134 features a T-tail with the horizontal stabilizer mounted high on the vertical fin, unlike the low-mounted tailplane of the Yak-42.
Tu-134 has low-mounted swept wings, whereas the 727-200 has a high-wing configuration.
Tu-134 possesses a slim, relatively short narrow-body fuselage compared to the longer fuselage of the MD-80.
Tu-134 has a pointed glazed nose profile giving a distinct bomber-like cockpit appearance, unlike the more rounded nose of the DC-9-30.
Tu-134 lacks underwing engine nacelles, showing a clean rear fuselage unlike the 727-200 which has three engines including two underwing units.
Tu-134 has a narrow-body fuselage cross-section smaller in diameter than the wider fuselage of the Yak-42.
Tu-134 features a single main landing gear unit per side with two wheels, whereas the DC-9-30 uses a dual-wheel main gear with a different strut geometry.
Tu-134 has a shorter overall length than the 727-200, making its fuselage proportionally more compact.
Tu-134 has no dorsal fin extension behind the vertical stabilizer, unlike the prominent dorsal fin on the MD-80.
Tu-134 has a narrower wing chord and less pronounced wing root fairing than the Yak-42.
Tu-134 has a forward fuselage that tapers sharply toward the nose, more so than the gently sloping nose of the DC-9-30.
Tu-134 has only two engines total, distinguishing it from the trijet 727-200 which has three visible engines.
Tu-134 has a vertical stabilizer with a straight leading edge and no anhedral, unlike the Yak-42’s slightly swept and anhedralled fin.
Tu-134 has passenger doors located only on the left side of the forward and mid-fuselage, with no rear door—unlike the 727-200 which includes a rear airstair door.
Tu-134 has a shorter distance between the trailing edge of the wing and the leading edge of the horizontal stabilizer than the MD-80.
Tu-134 has a fuselage that appears visually shorter relative to wing span than the DC-9-30, giving a more compact impression.
Tu-134 has a smooth, uninterrupted rear fuselage contour without the pronounced rear pressure bulkhead bulge seen on the Yak-42.
Tu-134 has a wing with moderate sweep angle, less than the sharper sweep of the MD-80 wing.
Tu-134 has a cockpit canopy with deeply recessed side windows and a steeply raked windshield, differing from the flatter, more upright cockpit glazing of the 727-200.
Tu-154: Tu-154 has three turbofan engines, with one mounted at the base of the vertical tail and two under the rear fuselage.
Tu-154 features a T-tail empennage where the horizontal stabilizer is mounted high on the vertical fin.
Tu-154 has low-mounted swept wings with moderate sweep angle and no winglets.
Tu-154 possesses a long, slim narrow-body fuselage proportionally longer than the Yak-42 but shorter than the DC-9-30.
Tu-154 has main landing gear housed in large, prominent fairings near the wing roots and lower rear fuselage.
Tu-154 exhibits a conventional non-widebody cross-section with evenly spaced cabin windows in a single straight row.
Tu-154 has a pointed, slightly drooping nose profile distinct from the blunter nose of the MD-80.
Tu-154 features rear-mounted engines, unlike the wing-mounted engines of the 727-200.
Tu-154 has a taller vertical tail relative to fuselage height compared to the DC-9-30.
Tu-154 displays a straight, unbroken dorsal spine line extending from cockpit to tail, unlike the stepped spine of the 727-200.
Tu-154 has a narrower fuselage diameter than the 727-200, visible in side profile cross-section.
Tu-154 features a single forward passenger door on the left side, positioned just ahead of the wing leading edge.
Tu-154 has no overwing emergency exits, distinguishing it from the MD-80 which has multiple overwing exits.
Tu-154 has a more tapered rear fuselage section ending in a sharp engine-intake transition at the vertical fin base.
Tu-154 has a deeper rear fuselage contour beneath the tail compared to the shallower taper of the Yak-42.
Tu-154 features a fixed, non-retractable ventral fin below the rear fuselage, absent on the DC-9-30 and MD-80.
Tu-154 has a longer nose section ahead of the cockpit windows than the Yak-42.
Tu-154 has a straight, uninterrupted wing root fairing without the pronounced bulge seen on the 727-200’s wing root.
Tu-154 has a higher-mounted horizontal stabilizer relative to the vertical fin height than the DC-9-30.
Tu-154 has a narrower chord vertical tail with a more acute leading edge sweep than the broader, straighter trailing edge of the MD-80’s fin.
Yak-42: Yak-42 has three jet engines: two mounted on the rear fuselage sides and one fed by a dorsal intake at the base of the vertical tail.
Yak-42 features a T-tail empennage with the horizontal stabilizer mounted high on the vertical fin.
Yak-42 has low-mounted swept wings with moderate sweep angle and no winglets.
Yak-42 has a slim, medium-length narrow-body fuselage that is shorter than the DC-9-30 and longer than the Tu-134.
Yak-42 has a pointed nose profile distinct from the rounded nose of the Tu-134.
Yak-42 has main landing gear mounted under the wing roots and forward fuselage area, not on long rear-fuselage stalks like the 727-200.
Yak-42 has a single forward passenger door ahead of the wing and no overwing exits.
Yak-42 has a dorsal engine intake that forms a prominent raised ridge along the upper rear fuselage centerline.
Yak-42 has a vertical tail with a straight leading edge and no rudder tab cutout, unlike the curved leading edge of the MD-80 tail.
Yak-42 has a cockpit canopy with a steeply raked windshield and a flat upper fuselage contour just aft of the cockpit.
Yak-42 has no auxiliary power unit (APU) inlet on the rear fuselage underside, unlike the 727-200.
Yak-42 has a narrow-body cross-section visibly slimmer than the DC-9-30 when viewed head-on.
Yak-42 has wing root fairings that blend smoothly into the fuselage without pronounced bulges, unlike the MD-80’s pronounced root fairings.
Yak-42 has a rear fuselage that tapers gradually to the tail without the abrupt narrowing seen on the Tu-134.
Yak-42 has engine nacelles with circular inlets and no visible thrust reverser sleeves on the rear fuselage engines.
Yak-42 has a vertical tail height proportionally greater relative to fuselage length than the 727-200.
Yak-42 has no ventral fin beneath the rear fuselage, unlike the DC-9-30.
Yak-42 has a forward fuselage that slopes downward gently from cockpit to nose, contrasting with the steeper drop of the Tu-134.
Yak-42 has wing-mounted pylons that attach directly to the lower wing surface without extended struts, unlike the 727-200’s strut-mounted engines.
Yak-42 has a dorsal intake that extends forward from the vertical tail base with a smooth, continuous curve, not segmented or squared like some DC-9 variants.
